source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs acting as flight-booking assistants barely improve over 5 rounds of observing a user's choices. A Bayesian Assistant (exact posterior over user reward functions) improves a lot.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 3 runs each, 100 new option sets tested per round. Bayesian Assistant 58% after round 1, 81% after round 5; random 37%. Models: Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Most LLMs near 37-45% after round 5 and nearly flat from round 1 (read from figure labels).
quote: LLMs fall far short of the standard defined by the Bayesian framework
limits: Synthetic user with a 4-feature linear reward; 5 rounds; simulated users give perfectly consistent choices.
agent_relevance: Plain LLMs do not accumulate evidence across turns like a Bayesian. Do not trust a model to hold a running posterior in its head.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching, CoT and prompting controls (appendix C.1)
finding: Prompt-level fixes did not repair belief updating. Chain-of-thought, numeric option encoding, 30 instead of 5 rounds, non-interactive few-shot format, and base (pre-instruct) models gave no meaningful improvement.
numbers: CoT ('Let's think step by step') accuracy similar to the default prompt (Fig 9a). A two-stage prompt that verbalizes a posterior over reward functions left direct prediction accuracy about the same; belief-derived predictions improved only in some settings.
quote: LLMs prompted with CoT perform similarly to those prompted in the way described in the main text
limits: Tested mainly on Gemma 2 9B; per-prompt numbers are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: CoT and explicit 'reason about the user' prompts are not a fix for sequential belief updating. Supports guardrails G10 and G11 (reasoning text is not evidence; think briefly).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian teaching by fine-tuning
finding: Fine-tuning an LLM to imitate the Bayesian Assistant's predictions beats fine-tuning on the correct answers (oracle teaching). Fine-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time.
numbers: Final-round accuracy of Bayesian-tuned Gemma and Llama about 75-76% (figure labels) vs Bayesian Assistant 81%; oracle-tuned and original models clearly lower. All differences p<0.001; 3 seeds x 3 training runs.
limits: Needs training data from an exact Bayesian model; flight task has a small known hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: Not usable by a scaffold-only agent (no training) but shows the target behaviour. Soft, graded feedback from a posterior teaches more than hard labels.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) generalization of Bayesian teaching
finding: The skill transferred to 2-8 flight features, to hotel recommendation, to a web-shopping domain with real products, and to real human users. Performance relative to the Bayesian Assistant dropped only moderately as features grew.
numbers: With human participants as users, all models including the Bayesian Assistant stayed well below the ~80% seen with simulated users, because human choices were not always consistent with stated preferences. For perfectly consistent humans the Bayesian LLM did much better than the original LLM.
limits: Human-user results noisy; the ceiling is set by user inconsistency.
agent_relevance: A normative teaching signal can generalize across domains. Noise in real users caps any Bayesian approach.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) human participants as the assistant
finding: Humans acting as the recommender improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002, logistic mixed-effects model) and beat small LLMs, but stayed below the Bayesian Assistant.
numbers: 48 of the 624 simulated users were given to human participants; humans slightly worse than larger LLMs, better than small ones.
limits: Small subset; humans were not Bayesian-optimal either.
agent_relevance: Human baseline is itself sub-Bayesian, so Bayesian optimality is an upper bound, not the target for a human-like agent.

source: Lin, Dai, Xing et al. (2026) AdaptFuse: training-free sequential preference inference via externalized Bayesian computation
finding: Keep the posterior outside the LLM. A symbolic module holds a Bayesian posterior over a discrete hypothesis set, a frozen LLM gives semantic likelihoods via multi-sample Dirichlet aggregation, and the two are fused by entropy. This matches or beats Bayesian Teaching with no fine-tuning.
numbers: Flight, Gemma 2 9B, final round: self-consistency 44.7%, Oracle Learning 59.1%, Bayesian Teaching 73.4%, AdaptFuse 76.2% (legacy config; 74.0% in the revised run, 52.3% in round 1). Also Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, hotel and web shopping. 3 samples give 73.3% at 2.63 s; fixed 50/50 fusion 72.7%; majority vote 73.1%.
quote: externalizes probabilistic computation entirely from the LLM
limits: Needs an enumerable hypothesis set designed per domain; a misspecified hypothesis grid still reached about 69-70%. Numbers shifted between preprint versions.
agent_relevance: Most directly usable pattern: offload belief arithmetic to code, use the LLM only for likelihood and semantics. Fits selection by prior and fit in a scaffold.

source: Batista & Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: A Bayesian agent fed data sampled from its own current hypothesis grows more confident but gains no ground truth. A Wason 2-4-6 experiment shows default chatbot behaviour acts like confirming evidence.
numbers: N=557 (Prolific), 3 rounds. Discovery rate: random-sequence feedback 29.5%, rule-disconfirming 14.1%, agreeable 11.8%, rule-confirming 8.4%, default GPT 5.9%. Default GPT vs random: diff 23.6 pp, p<.001. Default GPT vs disconfirming: diff 8.2 pp, p=.043. Confirming vs disconfirming not significant (p=.143).
limits: One task (2-4-6), one chatbot, hypotheses coded by an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite). Preprint.
agent_relevance: A model that samples evidence from the user's hypothesis is not independent evidence. Do not let a draft's own claims count as confirming data (G10); prefer tests sampled from the world.

source: Jagadish, Thalmann, Coda-Forno, Binz, Schulz (2025) Meta-learning ecological priors from LLMs explains human learning and decision making (ERMI)
finding: LLMs generate naturalistic learning tasks; a meta-learned network trained on them (ERMI) acts as a Bayesian-like learner with a learned prior and fits human trial-by-trial data better than classical cognitive models.
numbers: 15 experiments across function learning, category learning and decision making. Beats several established models by posterior model frequency. Function-learning extrapolation MMSE for ERMI 0.0223. Fitted inverse temperature 0.9 for ERMI vs 0.1 for meta-learned baseline MI in one test.
limits: LLMs used only as task generators; LLMs used directly as behaviour models fit worse (SI Fig S5). Feature choice still needs researcher judgement.
agent_relevance: Priors can be got from LLM-simulated worlds instead of hand-written. One answer to the problem of the priors.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: Earlier ERMI paper for category learning. A network meta-trained on LLM-generated categorisation tasks explains human data better than seven other cognitive models in two experiments and finds the same tasks hard as people do.
numbers: Logistic regression ceiling accuracy about 75% on both LLM-generated and real-world classification tasks; best rival model won human data less than 10% of the time in one comparison.
limits: Only category learning; human datasets were existing lab studies.
agent_relevance: The LLM-as-environment-prior idea works; can build priors over task types for an agent.

source: McCoy & Griffiths (2023) Modeling rapid language learning by distilling Bayesian priors into artificial neural networks
finding: Meta-training a neural net on many languages drawn from a Bayesian prior puts the prior inside the weights. It then learns formal languages as data-efficiently as a symbolic Bayesian learner.
numbers: 56 held-out formal languages (Yang and Piantadosi). A standard net needs about 10 times as many examples as the Bayesian learner for the same F-score; the prior-trained net matches the Bayesian learner. 40 re-runs per condition; n from 1 to 10,000 strings.
limits: Natural-language gains are small when data is large (8.5M words, perplexity only slightly better); gains show with small data or out-of-distribution tests (recursion, priming).
agent_relevance: Strong priors can be distilled into a flexible learner. Same idea as treating LLM pretraining as the prior and the prompt as evidence.

source: Griffiths, Zhu, Grant, McCoy (2023) Bayes in the Age of Intelligent Machines
finding: Argues Bayesian models and neural networks sit at different Marr levels and complement each other. Bayes gives a computational-level account of what a net should do and a way to read opaque LLMs.
numbers: No new experiments; summarises prior-distillation work.
limits: Position paper. Does not show that LLMs compute Bayesian posteriors.
agent_relevance: Use Bayes as a specification and audit tool for the agent, not as a claim about LLM internals.

source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang, Ma (2022) An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
finding: Proves in-context learning can emerge if pretraining text is a mixture of latent concepts (HMM mixture) and the prompt lets the model infer the shared concept. Tested on the synthetic GINC set.
numbers: GINC with transformers and LSTMs, 5 pretraining runs. With one concept (no mixture prior) in-context curves are flat. Random pretraining data: ICL fails. Unseen concepts: ICL fails. 12 to 16 layers: accuracy 81% to 85% at the same 1.33 pretraining loss. Zero-shot sometimes beats few-shot; example order matters.
limits: Synthetic small-scale data; theory needs the prompt close to pretraining distribution. Does not show real LLMs do exact Bayes.
agent_relevance: Prompt examples act as evidence for a latent concept, so example choice and order matter more than their number.

source: Falck, Wang, Holmes (2024) Is In-Context Learning in LLMs Bayesian? A Martingale Perspective
finding: Tests the martingale property (a necessary condition for any Bayesian learner on exchangeable data). LLMs violate it, so ICL is not exactly Bayesian.
numbers: Bernoulli tasks with n=50 observed samples, sample paths of length m=n/2 and 2n, true p in {.3,.5,.7}. Short paths mostly within the Bayesian CI except GPT-4; longer paths show more frequent violations. Gaussian task (n=100, m=50): all models except GPT-3.5 deviate. Models: GPT-3 170B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B. Uncertainty also did not shrink as Bayesian scaling predicts.
quote: We presented stark evidence that state-of-the-art LLMs violate the martingale property
limits: Small synthetic tasks, which the authors state as a limitation.
agent_relevance: Do not read LLM confidence as a posterior. Check with an external estimator.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of LLMs using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: Chain GPT-4 predictions in an iterated-learning loop; the chain converges to the model's implicit prior. Elicited priors qualitatively match human priors in causal strength, proportion estimation and six everyday quantities (lifespan, movie gross, poem length, pharaoh reign, runtime, cake time).
numbers: Modes of GPT-4 and human priors matched in all six everyday-quantity tasks; elicited priors explained GPT-4's own decisions better than a uniform prior in the causal and proportion tasks. Human comparison was by visual inspection of published plots.
limits: No quantitative fit statistics against human data; GPT-4 only; used on speculative events where there is no ground truth.
agent_relevance: A concrete probe for the agent's prior: iterate predictions to see what the model assumes before evidence arrives.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition
finding: Founding study. People predict totals from partial information (for example life span from current age) with median predictions close to Bayesian-optimal answers computed from real-world distributions (Gaussian, power-law, Erlang priors), with no parameters fitted to the human data.
numbers: 350 undergraduates: 208 predicted movie grosses, poem lengths, life spans, pharaoh reigns, marriage lengths; 142 predicted movie runtimes, terms of US representatives, cake baking times, waiting times, marriage lengths. Five values of t per phenomenon, varied between subjects.
quote: inconsistent with claims that cognitive judgments are based on non-Bayesian heuristics that are insensitive to priors
limits: Group medians only. Priors came from public data, not from the same people.
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim that human judgment tracks real-world priors.

source: Mozer, Pashler, Homaei (2008) Optimal Predictions in Everyday Cognition: The Wisdom of Individuals or Crowds?
finding: Challenge: the group accuracy can arise if each person holds only a tiny sample (k=2 remembered instances) of the relevant distribution; averaging then looks Bayesian.
numbers: A heuristic MinK model with k=2 instances reproduced the Griffiths & Tenenbaum group data and matched the variability of the data better than a model with veridical priors.
limits: Meant as a counter-model, not a psychological theory. Tested by iterated learning in c17.
agent_relevance: A Bayesian-looking aggregate can come from a cheap sampling rule. Two-sample heuristics may be enough in some cases.

source: Lewandowsky, Griffiths, Kalish (2009) The wisdom of individuals: exploring people's knowledge about everyday events using iterated learning
finding: Iterated-learning chains converge to the predicted priors. This fits Griffiths & Tenenbaum's Bayesian model and contradicts the MinK model, so individuals hold fairly rich knowledge of event distributions.
numbers: Reported as inconsistent with MinK predictions; stationary distributions of chains matched real-world priors (qualitative in the text read).
quote: accurate predictions about everyday events reflect relatively sophisticated knowledge on the part of individuals
limits: Rests on chain convergence; other small-sample models remain possible.
agent_relevance: Iterated learning is a usable way to measure a prior, in people or in an LLM (c14).

source: Bowers & Davis (2012) Bayesian just-so stories in psychology and neuroscience
finding: Main critique: priors, likelihoods and utility functions can be tuned after the fact so Bayesian models are unfalsifiable; they are rarely compared with non-Bayesian rivals that fit as well; neural evidence is weaker still.
numbers: Worked case: G&T 2006 life-span predictions could come from knowing that life expectancy is about 75 and ignoring current age; the 2-instance model fitted as well. Reviews memory, motion perception and reasoning where non-Bayesian accounts fit.
quote: the empirical evidence for Bayesian theories in psychology is weak
limits: Griffiths, Chater, Norris, Pouget (2012) reply that the goal is rarely to show optimality. Only the critique was opened here.
agent_relevance: A Bayesian scaffold must beat a simple baseline on the same data. A prior fitted after the fact proves nothing.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on classic judgement tasks. It falls for the conjunction fallacy (Linda) like people, but gets the cab base-rate problem approximately right, unlike people. Tiny prompt changes break it.
numbers: Black Cab variant (15% blue, 85% green cabs, asked about a black cab): GPT-3 answered 20%. Reversing Wason card order led to wrong selection. All three CRT items answered with the intuitive wrong answer. 13,000 decisions-from-description problems compared with human regret. Fails causal reasoning task.
quote: small perturbations to vignette-based tasks can lead GPT-3 vastly astray
limits: GPT-3 (2022); may have seen these vignettes in training. Adversarial variants cause large changes.
agent_relevance: A right answer on a famous vignette does not show a working base-rate mechanism. Test with perturbed items.

source: Liu, Geng, Peterson, Sucholutsky, Griffiths (2025) LLMs Assume People Are More Rational Than We Really Are
finding: LLMs predict human choices as if people maximised expected value, more than people do. Their inferences from others' choices resemble how humans infer, by assuming rationality.
numbers: Forward task with CoT: GPT-4o Spearman 0.94 with max expected value; humans 0.48. Correlation with human choices: GPT-4-Turbo 0.41, GPT-4o 0.28 (MSE 0.27 and 0.36). Llama-3-8B already 0.57 with EV. Inverse inference correlation with rational model: 0.20 for Llama-3-8B zero-shot vs 0.95 for GPT-4o CoT. Also GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3-70B, Claude 3 Opus.
quote: assume that people are more rational than we really are
limits: Gamble-choice dataset (Peterson et al.); CoT raises rationality and lowers human fit.
agent_relevance: If the agent models users, expect an over-rational prior on the user. Correct it with human data.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like Few-Shot Learning via Bayesian Reasoning over Natural Language
finding: An LLM proposes hypotheses in natural language, then they are reweighted by a prior and likelihood (Bayesian inference over language). Fits human number-game and set-concept judgments.
numbers: Held-out human number-game judgments: R2 = 0.95 with tuned prior and 100 samples; 50-100 hypotheses suffice (the original number game used over 5000); ablating the LLM proposal, or using Python hypotheses, fits worse; GPT-4 direct judgments were decidedly different from humans.
quote: GPT-4's judgments are decidedly different from humans
limits: Prior tuned on human data; optimising for task accuracy lowers fit to humans.
agent_relevance: Pattern for the agent: LLM proposes, an explicit prior and likelihood select. Tens of proposals suffice.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Combines an LLM hypothesis proposer with sequential Monte Carlo belief updating and expected-information-gain experiment design. Fuzzy (probabilistic) rules fit people; hard rules score higher but fit worse.
numbers: Zendo avg predictive posterior accuracy (of 8): human 5.26; direct LLM (ReAct) 4.60; batch fuzzy 5.35; online fuzzy 6.01; batch hard 6.55. Fit to human accuracy by rule: online fuzzy R2=.57, hard rules R2=.10, batch R2=.05, ReAct R2=.25. Per-judgment R2=.35. Log-likelihood of human data: best prior model -1539 vs batch fuzzy -1660.90. ActiveACRE task solving: 0.00 for the direct and some variants, up to 0.35 for the best hard-rule variant.
limits: Zendo-style board game and a synthetic benchmark; human data from Bramley et al.
agent_relevance: A running belief over LLM-proposed rules plus information-gain probes beat plain ReAct. Directly applicable to an impasse loop.

source: Ying, Zhi-Xuan, Wong, Mansinghka, Tenenbaum (2024) Grounding Language about Belief in a Bayesian Theory-of-Mind
finding: Bayesian inverse planning over goals and beliefs, with an LLM translating belief sentences into logic, predicts human goal and belief ratings much better than non-mentalizing baselines.
numbers: Correlation with human ratings: full BToM 0.93 [0.91, 0.94] for goal attributions and 0.92 [0.91, 0.93] for belief statements; with a uniform-over-statements prior 0.86; heuristic and non-mentalizing baselines 0.04-0.19 on belief statements; omniscient observer 0.64.
limits: Gridworld doors-and-keys with synthetic stimuli.
agent_relevance: LLM as parser, Bayesian engine as reasoner works in social inference.

source: Jin, Wu, Cao et al. (2024) MMToM-QA: Multimodal Theory of Mind Question Answering (BIP-ALM)
finding: BIP-ALM (Bayesian inverse planning with a language model supplying likelihoods) beats GPT-4V and GPT-4 on goal and belief questions, though it stays under human accuracy.
numbers: 600 questions over 134 videos. Overall accuracy, multimodal: human 93.0, GPT-4V 44.0, BIP-ALM with GPT-J 75.3, with LLaMA 2 76.7. Text only: human 82.5, GPT-4 48.0, SimToM with GPT-4 52.5, SymbolicToM with GPT-4 63.0, BIP-ALM GPT-J 71.7, LLaMA 2 70.5.
limits: Household simulator; two-choice questions so chance is 50%, and GPT-4 sits near chance overall.
agent_relevance: A small open model as the likelihood function inside a Bayesian wrapper beats a frontier model asked directly.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling
finding: An LLM samples candidate questions, a program translates them, and expected information gain picks the best. With k=10 samples it matches mean human performance; LLM-only questions are poorly grounded.
numbers: 18 boards. Human mean EIG 1.27; best human 3.61; 97% of human questions had EIG>0. Raw LLM questions (k=1) from CodeLlama and GPT-4 averaged EIG 0.65-0.66. LIPS with k=10 gives a close match to the human mean; GPT-4V gave no gain over text-only baselines.
limits: Single domain, single-turn questions; EIG needs an explicit board-state model.
agent_relevance: Sample-and-score by expected information gain turns noisy LLM questions into good ones with about ten draws. Fits impasse probing.

source: Handa, Gal, Pavlick, Goodman, Andreas, Tamkin, Li (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: Hybrid: Bayesian optimal experimental design picks features to ask about and an LM verbalises the questions. It improves preference elicitation over LM-only questioning and over BOED without a verbal interface.
numbers: Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA). OPEN beats LM-only baselines; removing the verbalisation step makes users significantly worse at specifying preferences. Open-ended LM questions score high under LM-based prediction, but OPEN's tracking of preferences outweighs that. Exact TIDA values are in a figure only.
limits: Content recommendation domain; exact effect sizes not read from text.
agent_relevance: Explicit uncertainty tracking plus a language interface beats free LLM questioning.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Models that ask open-ended questions or craft edge cases elicit task specifications more informative than user-written prompts or labels, in pre-registered studies.
numbers: Three domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning). Significant gain over baselines only in content recommendation and email verification; users found interactive elicitation less mentally demanding.
limits: Not a Bayesian method per se; no significance in moral reasoning.
agent_relevance: Asking informative questions beats waiting for a prompt, but the gain depends on the domain.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From Word Models to World Models: Translating from Natural Language to the Probabilistic Language of Thought
finding: An LLM translates utterances into probabilistic programs and Bayesian inference runs on them. Illustrated across probabilistic reasoning, relational, physical and social domains.
numbers: Illustrative case studies; no aggregate benchmark scores found in the text read.
limits: Qualitative; depends on the LLM generating correct code.
agent_relevance: LLM as translator, probabilistic engine as reasoner. Same pattern as AdaptFuse (c06).
